newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Retail sales, 30-yr T-bond sale.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Retail sales, 30-yr T-bond sale.

text.p: The U.S. government securities market gets its first major economic report of the week on Thursday, January retail sales figures that will serve as a prelude to the last leg of the Treasury's quarterly refinancing operation -- a $10.0 billion 30-year bond auction.

"Retail sales and (the January Producer Price Index on Friday) will be important, but retail sales will probably be more important to the market," said Peter D'Antonio, senior economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A.
"Retail sales is important because the direction of demand will dictate where we head in terms of economic growth in the first quarter," said D'Antonio.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that retail sales rose 0.7 percent in January and 0.6 percent when auto sales were excluded.

D'Antonio, who looks for a 0.6 percent retail sales gain overall and a 0.5 percent rise without auto sales, said some of that strength will be tied to strong apparel sales in New York State, sales spurred by a week-long suspension of the sales tax on clothing.
New York State accounts for about one-tenth of the nation's population and probably an even greater portion of its spending power, D'Antonio said.

Raphael Marrone, money market economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the market will also examine any revisions to the November and December retail sales numbers. Revisions to those months frequently accompany the January sales figures, economists said.
As for the January data, "we'll take a look at the level and see what it says about first-quarter personal consumption expenditures," Marrone said.
While the market is expected to focus on the retail sales report when it is released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, weekly jobless claims figures are also due at that time.
For the week ended February 8, economists expect new jobless claims to rise to 339,000 from 325,000 a week earlier.
"All evidence points to tight labor markets," Marrone said.
As soon as the market has absorbed the morning's economic data, it will shift its focus to the Treasury's $10.0 billion 30-year bond auction. The bidding deadline for the sale is 1300 EST/1800 GMT.

Participants were divided on the auction's prospects. Some said the Street holds much of the three- and 10-year notes that the Treasury sold in the first two parts of its refunding on Tuesday and Wednesday, respectively.
But others said prices had held up remarkably well as the new supply came to market.

"Our attitude here is mildly bullish," said Dana Johnson, First Chicago Capital Markets Inc. "But the Street seems to be taking on the supply OK. The auctions have been a little sloppy, a little lackluster. But the bid doesn't go away."
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended unchanged at 97-11/32 on Wednesday, yielding 6.71 percent.

"We think the economic reports are going to keep people pretty comfortable with the idea that the Fed is going to be on hold for a while and with the auctions out of the way, the market might be able to do a little better," said Johnson.
Federal funds were expected to open at 5-3/16 percent on Thursday, the first day of a new two-week bank reserve maintenance period, dealers indicated.
